disclaimer: This report is for educational and wellness purposes only. It is not a medical diagnosis and does not replace advice from a qualified healthcare professional. HbA1c results should be confirmed by your doctor. Do not start, stop or change any medication without medical advice.

status.label: In the diabetes range
status.explanation: Your HbA1c is 6.5% or above, the range used to diagnose diabetes. A single result is not a diagnosis: your doctor will confirm it with a repeat test or another blood test.

summary: Your HbA1c of 8.4% is in the diabetes range, and together with your age and low activity level, this suggests it's a good time to focus on steady, supportive habits. Your existing kidney condition is an important factor to keep in mind, since it affects how your body manages blood sugar and which foods and activities are safest for you. The most valuable next steps are getting your kidney function and urine tests, blood pressure, vitamin B12, and cardiovascular risk checked, staying consistent with light daily movement, and following the protein and potassium guidance in your diet plan. Working closely with your doctor on these points can help you manage things well over time.

comorbidity_assessment.note: The kidneys help clear excess sugar and manage fluid balance, so blood glucose levels in the diabetes range can place extra strain on them. This is why regular kidney function monitoring and care with protein, potassium, and phosphorus intake are especially important for you.

constraints: Do not follow high-protein diets or take protein supplements; keep protein moderate unless your kidney doctor advises otherwise.
Do not use potassium-based salt substitutes; ask your doctor whether you need to limit potassium or phosphorus.

foods_to_eat: Low-potassium vegetables such as cabbage, cauliflower, carrots and green beans
Whole grains like broken wheat, millets and brown rice in moderate portions
Moong dal and other pulses in small, measured amounts
Soy milk and plain soy curd as plant-based alternatives
Fresh fruits that are lower in potassium, such as apples and pears, in small portions
Healthy fats from a small amount of mustard or sesame oil
Herbs and spices like cumin, turmeric, coriander and ginger for flavour instead of salt
foods_to_avoid: Sugary drinks, fruit juices and sweetened beverages
Deep-fried snacks like samosas, pakoras and puris
Refined flour products such as white bread, naan and maida-based sweets
High-potassium foods like bananas, oranges, potatoes and tomatoes in large amounts unless your doctor says it is fine
Processed and packaged foods high in sodium and phosphorus additives
High-protein foods in large portions, including excess dals, soy chunks or protein-rich packaged foods
plan.portion_guidance: Keep meals moderate in size using small bowls and katoris as a guide. Since kidney health needs attention, keep protein portions modest and spread evenly through the day rather than having large amounts at once. Fill half your plate with low-potassium vegetables, a quarter with whole grains, and keep pulses or soy foods to a small, measured portion.
plan.hydration: Drink water through the day as guided by your doctor, since fluid needs can differ when kidney health is a concern. Avoid sugary drinks and packaged juices, and choose plain water or infused water with cucumber or mint instead.
based_on: HbA1c in the diabetes range: low-glycaemic, high-fibre focus
kidney disease: moderate protein, no potassium-based salt substitutes

exercise: Start with 10-15 minutes of gentle walking most days and slowly build up over several weeks.
Add light seated or standing strength exercises, such as resistance band movements, on 2 days a week, keeping effort gentle given your kidney condition.
Since you are currently sedentary and 70 years old, progress very gradually and stop if you feel pain, breathlessness, or dizziness.
Avoid regular use of painkillers such as ibuprofen for muscle soreness without checking with your healthcare provider first, as this is especially important with kidney disease.
lifestyle.walking_goal: Begin with a 10-minute walk, 5 days a week, and gradually build up to around 20-30 minutes most days of the week, as comfortable.
lifestyle.weight_management: Your BMI is in the normal range, so the focus should be on maintaining your current weight through balanced, consistent eating and regular gentle activity rather than trying to lose weight.
lifestyle.sleep: Aim for 7-9 hours of sleep each night. Try to keep a consistent bedtime and wake time, limit screens in the hour before bed, and keep your bedroom cool, dark, and quiet.
stress: Practice slow, deep breathing for 5 minutes a day, especially in the morning or before bed.
Try gentle seated stretching or meditation to help relax your body and mind.
Stay connected with family or friends regularly, as social contact can help lower stress.
behaviour_change: Keep a simple daily log of your walking and meals to track steady progress and stay motivated.
Work with your healthcare team to monitor your kidney function regularly, since this will help guide safe activity and dietary choices.
Avoid taking over-the-counter painkillers like ibuprofen regularly without medical advice, as these can affect kidney health.

monitoring.name: Kidney function (eGFR) and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio
monitoring.why: High glucose and blood pressure can quietly damage the kidneys; these tests find it early.
monitoring.frequency: Every year, or more often if you already have kidney disease

monitoring.name: Vitamin B12
monitoring.why: Metformin, a common diabetes medicine, can lower B12 over time; low B12 can mimic nerve damage.
monitoring.frequency: Ask your doctor, especially if you take metformin (often checked yearly)
risk_indicators: Vegetarian or vegan diet (lower dietary B12)

monitoring.name: Blood pressure
monitoring.why: High blood pressure multiplies the heart and kidney risks of high blood glucose.
monitoring.frequency: At every doctor visit; at home regularly if you have high blood pressure

monitoring.name: Cardiovascular risk assessment
monitoring.why: Heart disease is the leading cause of death in people with diabetes.

monitoring.name: HbA1c
monitoring.why: Shows your average blood glucose over about 3 months and whether your plan is working.
monitoring.frequency: Every 3 months until your doctor says you are at target, then every 6 months

monitoring.name: Fasting blood sugar
monitoring.why: Shows your blood glucose after an overnight fast and complements HbA1c.
monitoring.frequency: Alongside your HbA1c test, or as your doctor advises

monitoring.name: Post-meal (post-prandial) blood sugar
monitoring.why: Shows how your body handles glucose after meals, which HbA1c alone can hide.

monitoring.name: Lipid profile (cholesterol)
monitoring.why: Diabetes and high cholesterol together raise the risk of heart disease and stroke.
monitoring.frequency: Every year (at least every 5 years if you are under 40), or as your doctor advises
risk_indicators: Existing cholesterol problem or heart disease

monitoring.name: Vitamin D
monitoring.why: Low vitamin D is more common with obesity and kidney disease; testing is not routine for everyone.
monitoring.frequency: Only if your doctor recommends it

monitoring.name: Dilated eye examination
monitoring.why: Diabetes can damage the retina (diabetic retinopathy) long before your vision changes.
monitoring.frequency: Soon after diabetes is confirmed, then every year (your eye doctor may extend this to every 2 years if exams stay clear)

monitoring.name: Foot examination
monitoring.why: Diabetes can reduce feeling and blood flow in the feet, so small injuries go unnoticed.
monitoring.frequency: A full exam every year; check your own feet daily

preventive_actions: Schedule a kidney function (eGFR) and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio test soon, since this is a highlighted priority for you.
Add gentle, regular movement to your day, such as short walks, to help counter low activity levels.
Keep protein intake moderate and avoid protein supplements, following your diet plan's guidance.
Avoid potassium-based salt substitutes and regular use of painkillers like ibuprofen unless your doctor says it's safe.
Ask your doctor about checking blood pressure and vitamin B12 levels regularly, as these are flagged as high priority.

hba1c_caveat: HbA1c can be less accurate if you have anaemia, kidney disease, a recent blood transfusion or certain haemoglobin variants.
